Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient shows a partial radiologic response after intensive chemotherapy, with three lesions disappearing and the remaining lesions reduced by 40 % and becoming hypo‑intense on MRI, suggesting that a curative‑intent liver operation may be feasible. However, decisive information required to confirm technical resectability is missing: exact hepatic segments involved, size of the residual lesions, presence of vascular or biliary contact, and the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio. In addition, the status of the rectal primary (resected or not) and the presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (thoraco‑abdominal CT, peritoneal assessment) are unknown. Because these specific data are prerequisites for planning a safe hepatectomy, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending further evaluation.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy (e.g., complete the planned number of FOLFOXIRI cycles or consider adding targeted agents based on molecular profile once available) to maximize tumor shrinkage and increase the chance of a complete (R0) liver resection.  
- Obtain comprehensive staging:  
  • Triphasic liver CT or contrast‑enhanced MRI with volumetric analysis to define residual lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and calculate FLR.  
  • Thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, nodal, peritoneal, bone, or brain metastases.  
  • Pelvic MRI or endoscopic evaluation to determine whether the rectal primary has been resected or requires definitive treatment (radiotherapy or surgery).  
- If imaging confirms that all remaining liver disease can be removed with an adequate FLR (>30 % in a normal liver, >40 % in a chemotherapy‑injured liver), plan a parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (segmental/sectoral resections) possibly combined with intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult lesions.  
- If FLR is insufficient, consider pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (including ALPPS if appropriate) to induce hypertrophy before definitive resection.  
- Coordinate timing of rectal primary management:  
  • If the primary tumor is still in situ and symptomatic, prioritize neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by surgical resection (low anterior resection) either before or after liver surgery, depending on multidisciplinary consensus.  
  • If the primary is already resected, proceed directly to liver surgery after confirming resectability.  
- Post‑operative plan: adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of FOLFOXIRI or switch to maintenance) and regular CEA monitoring and imaging surveillance.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact hepatic segments involved, lesion dimensions, and presence of vascular/biliary invasion (critical for technical resectability and surgical planning).  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio or volumetric data (determines need for PVE or staged approach).  
- Status of the rectal primary tumor (resected vs. pending) and its molecular phenotype (RAS/BRAF) to guide targeted therapy and surgical sequencing.  
- Comprehensive extra‑hepatic staging (chest CT, peritoneal assessment, bone/brain imaging) to exclude contraindicating metastases.  
- Trend in CEA level after chemotherapy (helps assess biological response).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging and a chest CT scan.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI.
B. Precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
E. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor.
F. a chest CT scan
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation
I. Evolution of CEA after first-line chemotherapy.
J. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
Both recommendations address similar clinical domains: they assess resectability, suggest preoperative staging, outline systemic and surgical management, and mention postoperative treatment, thus achieving completeness alignment.

For step concordance, both recommendations identify the case as 'potentially resectable' and recommend a thorough restaging before any definitive surgical decision, aligning in how resectability and treatment plans are approached.

However, for case-tailoring, Recommendation 1 mentions the patient's molecular profile, FLR ratio, and specific monitoring details like CEA levels, which are less emphasized or differently discussed in Recommendation 2, which focuses more on the imaging aspects, including liquid biopsy considerations.

Regarding missing data concordance, both recommendations identify the need for detailed imaging and segmental analysis, FLR estimation, and status of the rectal primary. However, they differ in their emphasis on specific additional data; for instance, Recommendation 2 includes liquid biopsies and more extensive molecular profiling, which Recommendation 1 does not consider as critically missing data.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The liver MRI shows three residual lesions < 2 cm with a major radiologic response and no capsular infiltration, suggesting that a curative liver resection could be feasible. However, decisive information required to confirm technical and oncologic feasibility is missing:  
- Exact hepatic segments involved and any vascular or biliary contact (needed to plan parenchymal‑sparing resection and to assess risk of vascular reconstruction).  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio (required to ensure postoperative liver function).  
- Status of the primary rectal tumor (resected or not, need for neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms).  
- Comprehensive extra‑hepatic staging (chest‑CT, abdomen‑CT, pelvis imaging) to exclude pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases.  

Because these missing items are prerequisites for a safe and oncologically sound operation, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the required assessments.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (or PET‑CT) to rule out extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Obtain high‑resolution liver protocol CT or repeat MRI with volumetric analysis to define segmental location of each lesion, vascular/biliary relationships, and calculate FLR ratio.  
2. Evaluate and treat the primary rectal tumor  
   - If the rectal primary has not been resected, assess T/N stage with pelvic MRI.  
   - For locally advanced disease, deliver neoadjuvant long‑course chemoradiotherapy (or short‑course radiotherapy) followed by surgical resection (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection as indicated).  
   - If the primary is resectable and asymptomatic, consider simultaneous resection with liver surgery in a multidisciplinary setting.  
3. Plan liver surgery  
   - Assuming FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 20 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver) and no major vascular invasion, schedule a parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (e.g., wedge resections or limited segmental resections) to achieve R0 margins.  
   - Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and guide resection.  
   - If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) before definitive resection.  
4. Peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Continue the current chemotherapy regimen (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± biologic) for 2–3 cycles after liver resection as adjuvant therapy, given the initial high tumor burden.  
   - Consider adding anti‑EGFR therapy (cetuximab or panitumumab) in the adjuvant setting because the tumor is RAS wild‑type, provided no contraindications.  
5. Follow‑up  
   - Serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Exact hepatic segments involved, presence of vascular or biliary contact, and arterial anatomy.  
- Quantitative FLR ratio (volumetric assessment).  
- Status of the primary rectal tumor (resected vs. unresected, need for neoadjuvant therapy, presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms).  
- Full extra‑hepatic staging (chest CT, abdomen‑CT/pelvis MRI) to confirm absence of distant metastases.  
- Histologic grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (prognostic relevance).  

These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI and precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Status and treatment plan of the rectal primary tumor : Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
G. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
1. Completeness: Both recommendations are comprehensive, covering major clinical domains like resectability assessment, preoperative imaging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative follow-up. Recommendation 1 suggests additional imaging (PET-CT) and specific chemotherapy regimens, while Recommendation 2 delves into minimally invasive surgical approaches and prehabilitation strategies. Nevertheless, they address the same fundamental management components, thereby achieving completeness alignment.

2. Step Concordance: Both recommendations evaluate the case as potentially resectable due to partial response post-chemotherapy, though they provide slightly different rationales. Both propose staging before a potentially curative liver resection, with attention to systemic therapy. The sequence and actions, such as initial imaging, defining FLR, and liver resection strategy, are consistent across both recommendations, indicating concordance in clinical reasoning steps.

3. Case Tailoring Concordance: The recommendations differ in case-specific details. Recommendation 1 does not address certain specifics such as minimally invasive surgery, PRODIGE 23 protocol, or prehabilitation strategies outlined in Recommendation 2. Additionally, Recommendation 2 includes specific considerations like liquid biopsy analysis, which Recommendation 1 does not mention. This divergence indicates a lack of case-tailoring concordance.

4. Missing Data Concordance: Although both recommendations highlight the need for detailed liver mapping, FLR assessment, and rectal tumor status, they list different critical items. Recommendation 2 emphasizes mutation status and liquid biopsies, which are absent from Recommendation 1. This disparity suggests misalignment in missing data identification.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The only liver lesion that is progressing is 5 cm in segment VII. Whether it can be safely removed depends on (a) the vascular relationship of the lesion (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion – Missing), (b) the future liver remnant volume (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery – Missing), and (c) the presence of occult extra‑hepatic disease (ThoracoCTScanPerformed – False). In addition, the status of the primary colon tumour (Has the colorectal primary tumor been already resected? – Missing) influences the sequencing of surgery. Because these decisive pieces of information are absent, resection cannot be planned upfront and must be preceded by further staging and possibly additional systemic therapy.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Complete restaging  
   – Obtain a thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases (addressing the missing thoracic imaging).  
   – Perform a dedicated liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences and contrast‑enhanced vascular phase to define tumor‑vessel relationships, detect any additional occult lesions, and allow volumetric calculation of the future liver remnant.  
   – Review colonoscopy and/or abdominal imaging to confirm whether the primary left‑sided tumour has been resected; if not, schedule a curative colectomy (preferably before major liver surgery).  
• Systemic therapy  
   – Continue conversion chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) combined with bevacizumab, given KRAS mutation precludes anti‑EGFR agents.  
   – Re‑evaluate response after 2–3 additional cycles, monitoring CEA (CEALevel – Missing) and imaging.  
• Surgical planning (contingent on restaging)  
   – If extra‑hepatic disease is absent and FLR is ≥30 % (or ≥40 % in a steatotic liver) with adequate vascular anatomy, proceed to hepatic resection of the remaining six stable lesions and the progressing segment VII lesion, aiming for R0 margins.  
   – Consider intra‑operative ultrasound‑guided ablation (RFA/MWA) for lesions that are deep or adjacent to major vessels where resection would compromise FLR.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy the remnant before definitive hepatectomy.  
• Post‑operative management  
   – Resume adjuvant systemic chemotherapy for 3–6 months.  
   – Serial CEA and imaging follow‑up every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
• Thoraco‑CT or PET‑CT to rule out pulmonary metastases (ThoracoCTScanPerformed: False).  
• Liver MRI with vascular phase and volumetry to assess vascular invasion and FLR ratio (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion, ArterialAnatomy, FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery – Missing).  
• Status of the primary colorectal tumour (Has the colorectal primary tumor been already resected? – Missing) and any obstructive/bleeding symptoms.  
• Trend of tumor marker (CEALevel and CEALevelDecrease – Missing).  
These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial, residual, and disappeared lesions and detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Patient’s performance status for potential combined surgical/ablative strategy.
G. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
The two recommendations diverge significantly across all evaluated criteria.

1. **Completeness**: Recommendation 1 suggests the potentially resectable status with a detailed plan that includes preoperative restaging, systemic therapy, surgical intervention under certain criteria, and postoperative follow-up. Recommendation 2, however, labels the disease as unresectable due to heterogeneous response and emphasizes systemic therapy, with consideration for local treatments rather than a definitive surgical approach. The domains covered and the management components differ notably, with Recommendation 1 outlining a full surgical pathway and Recommendation 2 focusing on systemic control and selective local treatments.

2. **Step-by-Step Concordance**: The assessment of resectability differs: Recommendation 1 sees potential resectability depending on further evaluation, while Recommendation 2 deems the current status as unresectable. The subsequent management plans also diverge, with Recommendation 1 detailing a staged approach toward potential resection and adjuvant therapy, whereas Recommendation 2 advises on adapting systemic therapy and considers selective local treatments without committing to a resection strategy.

3. **Case-Tailoring Concordance**: Recommendation 1 primarily considers KRAS status affecting systemic therapy and FLR concerning surgical plans. Recommendation 2 delves into a broader range of patient-specific factors, including the tumor's molecular profile, performance status, and advanced molecular diagnostics like ctDNA and CTCs. These differences highlight the lack of alignment in case-specific tailoring across the recommendations.

4. **Missing Data Concordance**: While both recommendations identify the need for FLR evaluation and the primary tumor status, Recommendation 2 also stresses detailed lesion mapping, molecular profiling, patient performance status, and liquid biopsy data as critical missing pieces. Recommendation 1 focuses on more conventional staging data. The identified missing information does not fully align, indicating a gap in concordance.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: The current imaging shows a radiologic complete response of the bilobar liver metastases, but no liver lesions are visualized to be resected. Definitive surgical planning requires (a) confirmation that no occult residual disease remains in the liver (e.g., liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences or PET‑CT) and (b) clarification of the status of the rectal primary (already resected or still in situ). Because these decisive pieces of information are missing, resection cannot be performed upfront and must await further evaluation.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy as consolidation: complete the planned course of peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., additional 2–4 cycles of FOLFOXIRI or switch to a maintenance regimen) to consolidate the radiologic response.  
- Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI (including hepatobiliary contrast) and/or PET‑CT to exclude occult hepatic disease.  
- Clarify the status of the rectal primary:  
   • If the primary tumor has not been resected, proceed with standard rectal cancer management (long‑course chemoradiotherapy followed by total mesorectal excision, or upfront TME if already down‑staged).  
   • If the primary has already been resected with negative margins, continue surveillance.  
- Surveillance protocol after consolidation:  
   • CEA measurement every 6–8 weeks.  
   • Liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) every 2–3 months for the first year.  
   • Colonoscopic evaluation of the rectal site per standard guidelines.  
- If imaging subsequently reveals residual or recurrent liver disease, consider salvage hepatic surgery (parenchymal‑sparing resection) or local ablative techniques (RFA/MWA) depending on lesion location and future liver remnant.  
- Discuss the need for adjuvant chemotherapy (3–6 months) after completion of consolidation, especially if the primary tumor is high‑risk (poor differentiation, KRAS/BRAF mutation, MSI‑high).  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Primary tumor status (has the rectal cancer been resected? )  
- Histologic grade and molecular phenotype of the primary (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI)  
- Dedicated liver MRI (or PET‑CT) to rule out occult residual hepatic disease  
- Details of the original liver lesion burden (number, size, vascular contact) to assess future resection feasibility if disease recurs  
- Brain imaging status (to exclude occult cerebral metastasis)  
These items are essential to finalize the resectability decision and to tailor the subsequent oncologic plan.

• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach targeting the original metastatic locations, not only visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to detect occult residual disease.
• Depending on distribution, a staged approach may be required.

C. If surgical targeting of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and close imaging surveillance.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal strategy.

D. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• If surgery is performed, resume systemic therapy to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial lesions on baseline imaging.
B. Precise localization of the initial metastases relative to vascular structures.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor : circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, history of bisegmentectomy IV-V. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VII (3.9 cm). No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The lesion is solitary (1 metastasis, 3.9 cm, segment VII) and no extra‑hepatic disease is identified, which makes surgical removal feasible.  
- However, the Future Liver Remnant (FLR) ratio is not reported (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery: Missing). Adequate FLR is essential after a prior bisegmentectomy IV‑V; without this information the safety of a repeat hepatectomy cannot be confirmed.  
- Vascular or biliary involvement of the segment VII lesion is also missing, and these anatomic details could preclude a safe resection.  
- Because a decisive piece of information (FLR ratio) is lacking, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending further assessment.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete pre‑operative work‑up  
   - Obtain liver volumetry (CT or MRI) to calculate FLR; if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % in a steatotic liver) plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
   - Review contrast‑enhanced imaging to confirm absence of vascular or biliary invasion of the segment VII lesion.  
   - Verify status of the colorectal primary (has it been resected? location, pathology, CEA level) and assess for any occult extra‑hepatic disease, including a brain MRI (brain involvement is currently Missing).  
2. Systemic therapy  
   - KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR agents; standard peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) is appropriate.  
   - Because this is a late isolated hepatic recurrence, an upfront surgery approach is reasonable once FLR is confirmed, with adjuvant chemotherapy (6 cycles) administered post‑operatively.  
   - If FLR is insufficient and PVE is required, give 2–3 cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy while awaiting hypertrophy.  
3. Surgical plan  
   - Perform an anatomic segmentectomy of VII (or a non‑anatomic wedge resection) preserving the previous bisegmentectomy IV‑V.  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to verify lesion margins and exclude additional occult disease.  
   - Ensure negative margins (R0) and achieve adequate vascular control.  
4. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume adjuvant chemotherapy within 6–8 weeks if recovery is uneventful.  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Future Liver Remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric assessment (critical for safety of repeat hepatectomy).  
- Detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the segment VII lesion (to confirm resectability).  
- Status of the colorectal primary tumor (resected or pending, location, grade, CEA level).
